lead: A camera model is a set of equations that turns a 3D point into a pixel. The pinhole model uses two steps: a rigid transform from world to camera, then a perspective divide and scale to image coordinates. Calibration estimates the scale and origin (intrinsic) and the pose (extrinsic). Phone cameras, AR apps, robot arms and drone mapping need these numbers; without them a measured pixel cannot become a direction in space.
prereq: You need: image formation (see Unit 1, Foundations) and matrix multiplication with homogeneous coordinates.

blocks.text: A pinhole camera has a small opening and an image plane behind it. Light from a 3D point goes straight through the opening and hits one pixel. Put the camera centre at the origin of a camera frame, with the optical axis along +Z. The point has camera coordinates (X, Y, Z) in metres.

Similar triangles give the pixel. The pixel u grows with X and shrinks with Z: u = fx·X/Z + cx. The pixel v grows with Y and shrinks with Z: v = fy·Y/Z + cy. Here fx and fy are focal lengths in pixels; (cx, cy) is the principal point, the pixel where the optical axis meets the image. The division by Z is the perspective divide. A far object has large Z, so it moves few pixels.
u = fx·X/Z + cx,   v = fy·Y/Z + cy
blocks.where: (X, Y, Z) is the point in camera coordinates in metres; fx, fy are focal lengths in pixels; (cx, cy) is the principal point in pixels; (u, v) is the pixel coordinate.

blocks.text: Homogeneous coordinates add a 1: (X, Y, Z, 1). A 4×4 matrix can then hold translation. A 3×4 projection matrix maps a world point to homogeneous pixel (u', v', w'); dividing by w' gives (u, v). That matrix is P = K[R|t].

The intrinsic matrix K holds the camera's inside numbers: K = [[fx, 0, cx], [0, fy, cy], [0, 0, 1]]. fx and fy are in pixels, not millimetres. If the physical focal length is f metres and one pixel is p metres wide, fx = f/p. A phone camera may have fx = fy = 800 px, cx = 320 px, cy = 240 px on a 640×480 image. The principal point is near the image centre, but calibration measures it.

The extrinsic matrix holds the camera pose. Rotation R (3×3) and translation t (3×1) map a world point X<sub>w</sub> to camera coordinates: X<sub>c</sub> = R·X<sub>w</sub> + t. The camera centre in world coordinates is C = −Rᵀ·t. Extrinsic comes first, then intrinsic: move the world point into the camera frame, then project it to pixels.
P = K [R | t],   X<sub>c</sub> = R X<sub>w</sub> + t,   [u, v, 1]ᵀ ∝ K X<sub>c</sub>
blocks.where: P is the 3×4 camera matrix; K is the 3×3 intrinsic matrix; R is the 3×3 rotation; t is the 3×1 translation; X<sub>w</sub> is a world point; X<sub>c</sub> is the same point in camera coordinates; ∝ means equal after dividing by the third coordinate.

blocks.text: Some syllabi call finding R and t from image points camera resection. The same equations let a robot arm move to a point seen by a fixed camera.

A real lens bends straight lines near the image edge. Radial distortion scales the offset of a pixel from the principal point. First convert to dimensionless normalized image coordinates: x = (u − cx)/fx and y = (v − cy)/fy. Then r² = x² + y². The undistorted pixel is u<sub>undist</sub> = cx + (u − cx)·(1 + k1·r² + k2·r⁴), and v<sub>undist</sub> = cy + (v − cy)·(1 + k1·r² + k2·r⁴). Here k1 and k2 are radial coefficients; they apply to the normalized coordinates x and y. Tangential distortion adds p1 and p2 because the lens is not perfectly parallel to the sensor. These numbers are fitted after K and pose.

Checkerboard calibration uses a board with known square size, say 25 mm. The camera takes 10 to 20 images at different tilts. A corner detector finds inner corners; their 3D positions on the board are known. A direct linear transform (DLT) solves a projection matrix from six or more point pairs. Zhang's method uses each planar view's homography to constrain K, giving a closed-form first estimate; nonlinear least squares refines K, R, t and distortion. Only a few universities teach the closed-form steps in detail.

Reprojection error judges the fit: project every known 3D corner with the fitted camera and compare with the detected pixel. The per-corner error is the Euclidean distance in pixels between the detected and projected corner: e<sub>i</sub> = √((u<sub>obs,i</sub> − u<sub>pred,i</sub>)² + (v<sub>obs,i</sub> − v<sub>pred,i</sub>)²). Calibration tools report the root-mean-square error over all N corners, e = √((1/N)·Σ(du² + dv²)), where du and dv are the observed minus projected pixel differences. A good calibration often reaches well under 1 px. Large error means bad corners, too few views, or a board that was not rigid.

figure.caption: The point (1.0, 0.5, 2.0) m goes through the intrinsic matrix with fx = fy = 800 px and principal point (320, 240) px, landing at pixel (720, 440). Here R is the identity and t = 0, so the extrinsic step leaves the point unchanged.

spec.title: Pinhole projection
spec.aria: Pinhole projection from a world point through extrinsic rotation and translation, then the intrinsic matrix, to a pixel.

examples.question: A camera has fx = fy = 800 px, cx = 320 px, cy = 240 px. A point in camera coordinates is (X, Y, Z) = (1.0 m, 0.5 m, 2.0 m). Find its pixel (u, v).
steps: The point is already in camera coordinates, so R and t are not needed.
examples.answer: The point projects to pixel (u, v) = (720 px, 440 px).
examples.check:
fx = 800.0
fy = 800.0
cx = 320.0
cy = 240.0
X = 1.0
Y = 0.5
Z = 2.0
u = fx * X / Z + cx
v = fy * Y / Z + cy
print(u)
print(v)

traps: Putting focal length in millimetres into K. fx and fy in K are in pixels; divide the physical focal length by pixel pitch.
Forgetting the divide by Z. The raw homogeneous values are not pixels until you divide by the third coordinate.
Mixing world and camera coordinates. R and t must move the point into the camera frame before K is applied.
Using the image centre from sensor size as cx, cy. Calibration returns the measured principal point, which can be several pixels away.
Fitting distortion before K and pose. The usual order is K and pose from a linear model, then distortion, then joint refinement.

quiz.q: Write the pinhole equations for u and v. Define each symbol.
quiz.a: u = fx·X/Z + cx and v = fy·Y/Z + cy. (X, Y, Z) is the camera-coordinate point in metres; fx, fy are focal lengths in pixels; (cx, cy) is the principal point in pixels.

quiz.q: Why does a point at Z = 4 m produce half the pixel offset of the same X at Z = 2 m?
quiz.a: The offset is fx·X/Z. Doubling Z halves X/Z, so the pixel offset halves; perspective makes distant points look closer to the principal point.

quiz.q: fx = 1000 px, cx = 400 px, cy = 300 px. A camera-coordinate point is (2 m, 1 m, 4 m). Find (u, v).
Calibration reports 8 px reprojection error. Give two likely causes and one check.
quiz.a: Bad corner detection or too few board views; check corner overlays and add tilted views. A non-rigid board also causes this.

quiz.q: A physical focal length is 4 mm and the pixel pitch is 2 µm. Find fx in pixels.
How can a planar checkerboard determine K when each view has unknown pose?
quiz.a: Each view gives a homography. Homography entries are products of K and the plane's rotation and translation. Several views give enough constraints to solve K; Zhang's method does this linearly, then refines.

quiz.q: State the reprojection error for one corner.

beyond: Not for the exam. Camera calibration is built into OpenCV (calibrateCamera), ROS camera drivers, and ARKit/ARCore. Factory calibration of phone cameras uses large collimators and many poses. Research moves to self-calibration from natural scenes and deep networks that predict depth and intrinsics. Search for Zhang calibration, bundle adjustment, and camera intrinsics from EXIF.
